Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 44
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Retail Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Affective Expression: Crying, Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Event Recall: Talking about the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat, Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me, People Pleasing: go along with whatever others want to feel safe
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled
  Memory: Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Vignette:
Priya Sharma is a 44-year-old retail worker in a large suburban discount store, married for eighteen years. The event that shattered her sense of safety occurred nine months ago, on a Tuesday afternoon in early spring. She was stocking cleaning supplies in aisle six when she heard a commotion near the pharmacy counter. A middle-aged man had collapsed, his face a mottled purple, his hands clawing at his throat. A woman—his wife, Priya later learned—was screaming for help. Priya dropped her box of detergent and ran to get the store manager, but by the time they returned with the defibrillator, the man had stopped moving. Paramedics arrived within minutes, but they could not revive him. Priya stood frozen behind a display of vitamins, watching the wife sob over his body, watching the paramedics pack their equipment away. She did not know the man or his wife, but she has not stopped thinking about them since.

At first she told herself it was just shock, that she would get over it. But within a week she noticed changes she could not explain. When her husband, Raj, asked about her day at dinner, she tried to describe what had happened, but the words came out jumbled. She remembered the sound of the woman’s scream but not the order of what came next—the manager’s voice on the intercom, the sirens, the thud of the man’s body hitting the linoleum. The sequence felt scrambled, as if the memory had been torn apart and reassembled wrong. Talking about it made her dizzy, a floating sensation that left her gripping the edge of the kitchen counter. Raj stopped asking after she burst into tears the third time he brought it up. She now avoids any mention of the event, but the grief it carries still ambushes her: a wave of sorrow for a stranger that floods her chest without warning, so intense she has to stop whatever she is doing and breathe.

At work, Priya’s environment has become a landscape of threats. She constantly scans the aisles for signs of distress—a customer leaning against a shelf, a child coughing, an elderly person walking slowly. Her eyes dart from face to face, checking for the same panicked expression she saw that day. She is hypervigilant, unable to relax even in the break room, and she startles at the sharp beep of the cash register or the sudden clatter of a dropped item. The dizziness returns whenever she passes the pharmacy counter, so she now takes the long way to the stockroom, adding ten minutes to every trip. She has also noticed that she has become excessively agreeable at work and at home. She says yes to extra shifts she does not want, and agrees to plans Raj suggests even when she is exhausted, because refusing anyone feels unsafe—as if saying no could somehow provoke another catastrophe. She cannot explain the logic; she only knows that going along with what others want makes her feel momentarily less exposed.

Her preoccupation with why this happened has become almost constant. She replays the moment: Was she supposed to have noticed the man earlier? Could she have done something different—called 911 sooner, yelled louder? The questions circle without answers, and the lack of resolution deepens her sense that the world is unpredictable and that she is helpless in the face of it. She has come to believe that if she stays vigilant enough, if she checks every corner and placates everyone around her, she might prevent another tragedy. But she also knows, somewhere beneath that hope, that it is impossible.

The toll on her marriage has been quiet but real. Raj has grown frustrated with her constant scanning when they are out—at the grocery store, at a restaurant, she is always looking past him, searching for something she cannot name. She has stopped going to family gatherings because the noise and crowds overwhelm her. She feels guilty, but the fear of being caught off guard is stronger. It was Raj who finally suggested she talk to someone, after she woke him at 3 a.m. sobbing from a dream she could not fully remember, only that the man’s face had merged with her husband’s, and she had watched him fall and fall. She agreed because she is tired of being afraid, and because she wants—though she is not sure it is possible—to stop feeling that she is still standing in aisle six, watching a life end she never knew.
